Topic: Z-Transform and Region of Convergence

This page introduces the Z-transform as a mathematical tool used in Digital Signal Processing for the analysis of discrete-time signals. It establishes the analogy between the Laplace transform for continuous-time signals and the Z-transform for discrete-time signals, and it introduces the concept of the Region of Convergence (ROC).

In continuous-time analysis, the Laplace transform is defined using a complex variable ( s ). In discrete-time analysis, the Z-transform is defined using a complex variable ( z ). The complex variable ( z ) can be expressed in polar form as ( z = r e^{j\theta} ), where ( r = |z| ) is the magnitude and ( \theta ) is the phase angle. The set of all possible values of ( z ) forms the z-plane.

Definition of the Z-Transform

For a discrete-time sequence ( x[n] ), the Z-transform is defined as

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} )

In this definition, ( x[n] ) represents the signal in the time domain and ( X(z) ) represents its transform in the complex frequency domain. The term ( z^{-n} ) serves as the complex exponential basis function for discrete-time systems.

The infinite summation may not converge for all values of ( z ). Convergence depends on the magnitude of ( z ) and the behavior of ( x[n] ). The set of all values of ( z ) for which the summation converges is called the Region of Convergence (ROC).

Relationship with the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform

If we restrict ( z ) to lie on the unit circle by substituting ( z = e^{j\omega} ), then the Z-transform becomes

( X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] e^{-j\omega n} )

This expression is the definition of the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT). Therefore, the DTFT is a special case of the Z-transform evaluated on the unit circle defined by ( |z| = 1 ). The DTFT exists only if the unit circle lies within the ROC.

Example: Right-Sided Exponential Sequence

Consider the right-sided sequence ( x[n] = a^n u[n] ), where ( u[n] ) is the unit step sequence defined as 1 for ( n \ge 0 ) and 0 otherwise.

Substituting into the definition of the Z-transform gives

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a^n z^{-n} )

This can be rewritten as

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (a z^{-1})^n )

This is a geometric series with common ratio ( r = a z^{-1} ). A geometric series converges only when the magnitude of the ratio is less than 1. Therefore, the convergence condition is

( |a z^{-1}| < 1 )

Rearranging this inequality gives

( |z| > |a| )

Using the formula for the sum of a geometric series

( \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} r^n = \frac{1}{1 - r}, \quad |r| < 1 )

we obtain

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} )

Multiplying numerator and denominator by ( z ) to express the result as a rational function of ( z ), we get

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} )

The denominator becomes zero at ( z = a ), which indicates a pole at ( z = a ). The ROC is therefore the region ( |z| > |a| ), which corresponds to the exterior of a circle of radius ( |a| ) centered at the origin. The ROC does not include the pole.

Interpretation of the Region of Convergence

The ROC determines where the Z-transform exists. It is typically a circular region in the z-plane and is determined by the magnitude of ( z ). The ROC cannot include poles because the transform becomes unbounded at pole locations.

Depending on the nature of the sequence:

For right-sided sequences, the ROC lies outside the outermost pole and extends to infinity.

For left-sided sequences, the ROC lies inside the innermost pole and extends toward the origin.

For sequences that extend in both directions (two-sided sequences), the ROC lies between two circular boundaries.

For finite-duration sequences, the summation reduces to a finite number of terms, and therefore the ROC is generally the entire z-plane except possibly at ( z = 0 ) or ( z = \infty ), depending on the powers of ( z ).

This page establishes the mathematical formulation of the Z-transform, demonstrates how it reduces to the DTFT under unit circle substitution, and explains how convergence conditions determine the Region of Convergence in the z-plane.

Topic: Special Sequences and Inverse Z-Transform

This page continues the discussion of the Z-transform by analyzing specific discrete-time signals and their Regions of Convergence (ROC). It also introduces the concept of the inverse Z-transform.

Impulse Sequence

Consider the discrete-time impulse signal defined as ( x[n] = \delta[n] ). The impulse sequence is equal to 1 at ( n = 0 ) and 0 for all other values of ( n ).

Substituting into the definition of the Z-transform,

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta[n] z^{-n} )

Since ( \delta[n] ) is nonzero only at ( n = 0 ), the summation reduces to

( X(z) = z^{0} = 1 )

Thus, the Z-transform of the impulse signal is 1. Because this result does not involve an infinite summation, the transform converges for all values of ( z ). Therefore, the ROC is the entire z-plane.

Shifted Impulse Sequence

For a shifted impulse signal of the form ( x[n] = \delta[n - k] ), the Z-transform becomes

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta[n - k] z^{-n} )

The impulse is nonzero only when ( n = k ), so the summation reduces to

( X(z) = z^{-k} )

Since this is a finite expression, the ROC is the entire z-plane except possibly at ( z = 0 ) if negative powers are present.

Inverse Z-Transform

The page introduces the inverse Z-transform, which allows recovery of the original time-domain sequence ( x[n] ) from ( X(z) ). The inverse Z-transform is defined as

( x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi j} \oint_{C} X(z) z^{n-1} dz )

where ( C ) is a closed contour within the ROC in the complex z-plane. The contour integral ensures that the value of ( x[n] ) is uniquely determined by ( X(z) ) and the ROC.

Right-Sided Exponential Sequence

Consider again the right-sided exponential sequence ( x[n] = a^n u[n] ).

Its Z-transform is

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} )

with ROC given by ( |z| > |a| ).

This result shows that the transform has a pole at ( z = a ). The ROC extends outward from this pole and does not include it.

Interpretation of ROC in These Examples

For the impulse sequence, the ROC includes the entire z-plane because the transform is finite and contains no poles.

For shifted impulse sequences, the ROC remains the entire plane except possibly at singular points introduced by negative powers of ( z ).

For exponential sequences, the ROC depends on whether the sequence is right-sided or left-sided. In the right-sided case, the ROC lies outside the pole; in the left-sided case, the ROC lies inside the pole.

This page reinforces how the structure of the time-domain signal determines the algebraic form of ( X(z) ), the pole locations, and the corresponding Region of Convergence.

Topic: Properties of Region of Convergence and Combined Sequences

This page discusses how the Region of Convergence (ROC) behaves when multiple sequences are combined and how pole locations influence the ROC. The focus is on understanding how algebraic combinations in the Z-domain correspond to time-domain signal structures.

Z-Transform Representation

For a general discrete-time sequence ( x[n] ), the Z-transform is defined as

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} )

When sequences are expressed as sums of exponential components, the resulting Z-transform becomes a rational function in ( z ), typically of the form

( X(z) = \frac{N(z)}{D(z)} )

where ( N(z) ) and ( D(z) ) are polynomials in ( z ). The zeros of ( D(z) ) correspond to poles of the system.

Effect of Combining Sequences

If two sequences ( x_1[n] ) and ( x_2[n] ) are added together, their Z-transforms add:

( X(z) = X_1(z) + X_2(z) )

The Region of Convergence of the resulting transform depends on both individual ROCs. Specifically, the ROC of the sum is the intersection of the individual ROCs.

This means that only those values of ( z ) for which both ( X_1(z) ) and ( X_2(z) ) converge will belong to the ROC of the combined sequence.

Pole Interaction and ROC

If the combined Z-transform introduces multiple poles, the ROC must exclude all poles. The final ROC is determined by the outermost and innermost poles depending on whether the sequence is right-sided, left-sided, or two-sided.

If the resulting sequence is right-sided, the ROC extends outward from the pole of largest magnitude.

If the sequence is left-sided, the ROC extends inward toward the origin from the pole of smallest magnitude.

If the sequence is two-sided, the ROC lies between two poles, forming an annular region of the form

( R_1 < |z| < R_2 )

Interpretation of ROC When Sequences Are Combined

When signals are combined, their algebraic representation in the Z-domain may suggest multiple possible ROCs. However, the actual ROC is determined by the nature of the time-domain signal.

For example, if a rational function has poles at multiple locations, the ROC cannot include any of those poles. Depending on whether the signal is causal, anti-causal, or two-sided, the ROC will be chosen accordingly.

This page emphasizes that the ROC is not determined solely by the algebraic expression of ( X(z) ), but also by the time-domain behavior of ( x[n] ). The same algebraic expression may correspond to different sequences depending on the ROC.

Thus, specifying the ROC is essential for uniquely identifying the inverse Z-transform.

Topic: Linear Combination of Sequences and ROC Determination

This page discusses the linearity property of the Z-transform and demonstrates how the Region of Convergence (ROC) is determined when multiple exponential sequences are combined. It also presents an example involving rational Z-transforms with multiple poles and analyzes the corresponding ROC.

Linearity Property of the Z-Transform

If two sequences ( x_1[n] ) and ( x_2[n] ) have Z-transforms ( X_1(z) ) and ( X_2(z) ) respectively, then for constants ( a ) and ( b ),

( x[n] = a x_1[n] + b x_2[n] )

implies

( X(z) = a X_1(z) + b X_2(z) )

This property follows directly from the linearity of summation in the definition

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} ).

The ROC of the combined signal is the intersection of the individual ROCs of ( X_1(z) ) and ( X_2(z) ).

Example: Sum of Right-Sided Exponentials

Consider a signal composed of two right-sided exponential sequences:

( x[n] = A (a^n u[n]) + B (b^n u[n]) )

Using the known result for the Z-transform of ( a^n u[n] ),

( Z\{a^n u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - a}, \quad |z| > |a| )

Similarly,

( Z\{b^n u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - b}, \quad |z| > |b| )

Therefore,

( X(z) = A \frac{z}{z - a} + B \frac{z}{z - b} )

The poles are located at ( z = a ) and ( z = b ).

Since both sequences are right-sided, the ROC must extend outward from the outermost pole. Thus,

( |z| > \max(|a|, |b|) )

Example: Rational Z-Transform with Multiple Poles

Consider a rational function of the form

( X(z) = \frac{1}{(1 - 2z^{-1})(1 - 3z^{-1})} )

To express this in terms of positive powers of ( z ), multiply numerator and denominator by ( z^2 ):

( X(z) = \frac{z^2}{(z - 2)(z - 3)} )

The poles are at ( z = 2 ) and ( z = 3 ).

Possible ROCs

Since there are two poles, the ROC depends on the nature of the time-domain signal:

If the sequence is right-sided (causal), the ROC is

( |z| > 3 )

If the sequence is left-sided (anti-causal), the ROC is

( |z| < 2 )

If the sequence is two-sided, the ROC lies between the poles:

( 2 < |z| < 3 )

Thus, the algebraic expression alone does not uniquely determine the signal. The ROC must be specified to identify whether the sequence is right-sided, left-sided, or two-sided.

Conclusion

This page emphasizes that when combining sequences or working with rational Z-transforms, the pole locations determine possible ROCs. The actual ROC depends on the time-domain behavior of the sequence. Therefore, both ( X(z) ) and its ROC are required to uniquely determine ( x[n] ).

Topic: Z-Transform of Finite Sequences and ROC for Polynomial and Rational Functions

This page analyzes the Z-transform of finite-duration sequences and polynomial expressions in ( z^{-1} ). It also discusses how the Region of Convergence (ROC) is determined when the Z-transform contains only a finite number of terms or when it is expressed as a rational function.

Z-Transform of a Finite Sequence

Consider a finite-length discrete-time sequence such as

( x[n] = \{x[0], x[1], x[2], \dots, x[N]\} )

The Z-transform is given by

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} x[n] z^{-n} )

Since the summation contains only a finite number of terms, there is no issue of convergence due to infinite summation. Therefore, the ROC is the entire z-plane except possibly at ( z = 0 ) if negative powers of ( z ) are present.

If the sequence contains only nonnegative powers of ( z^{-1} ), then the transform is a polynomial in ( z^{-1} ). In such cases, the only possible singularity is at ( z = 0 ). Thus,

ROC: entire z-plane except possibly ( z = 0 ).

Example: Polynomial in ( z^{-1} )

If

( X(z) = 1 + 2z^{-1} + 3z^{-2} )

then this corresponds to a finite-duration sequence

( x[0] = 1, x[1] = 2, x[2] = 3 )

Since this is a finite polynomial expression, the ROC is the entire z-plane except ( z = 0 ).

Rational Z-Transform

Now consider a rational function of the form

( X(z) = \frac{P(z)}{Q(z)} )

where ( P(z) ) and ( Q(z) ) are polynomials in ( z ).

The values of ( z ) that make ( Q(z) = 0 ) are poles of the system. The ROC cannot include these pole locations.

Example: Rational Function with Multiple Poles

Suppose

( X(z) = \frac{z^2 + 4z + 5}{z(z - 2)(z - 4)} )

The poles occur at

( z = 0 ), ( z = 2 ), and ( z = 4 ).

Possible ROCs depend on the time-domain nature of the sequence:

If the sequence is right-sided (causal), the ROC is

( |z| > 4 )

If the sequence is left-sided (anti-causal), the ROC is

( |z| < 0 )

If the sequence is two-sided, the ROC lies between poles, for example

( 2 < |z| < 4 )

The ROC is always a connected region and cannot contain poles.

Shifted Sequences

If a sequence is shifted in time, such as

( x[n - k] )

its Z-transform becomes

( z^{-k} X(z) )

This multiplication by ( z^{-k} ) may introduce additional powers of ( z ) but does not change the pole locations except possibly introducing or removing a pole at ( z = 0 ). The ROC remains the same except for possible exclusion of ( z = 0 ).

General Observations

1. Finite-length sequences produce polynomial Z-transforms.
2. The ROC for finite sequences is typically the entire z-plane except possibly at ( z = 0 ).
3. Rational Z-transforms introduce poles.
4. The ROC cannot include poles.
5. The actual ROC depends on whether the sequence is right-sided, left-sided, or two-sided.

This page reinforces the principle that both the algebraic expression ( X(z) ) and its ROC are required to uniquely determine the time-domain sequence.

Topic: Time Scaling, Exponential Modulation, and Z-Transform of Cosine Sequence

This page discusses properties of the Z-transform related to scaling and exponential modulation. It also presents an example involving the Z-transform of a cosine sequence multiplied by a unit step sequence.

Scaling Property

If a discrete-time sequence ( x[n] ) has Z-transform ( X(z) ), then multiplying the sequence by an exponential term results in a scaling transformation in the Z-domain.

If

( x[n] \xleftrightarrow{Z} X(z) )

then

( a^n x[n] \xleftrightarrow{Z} X\left( \frac{z}{a} \right) )

This property follows from the definition of the Z-transform:

( Z\{a^n x[n]\} = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} a^n x[n] z^{-n} )

Rewriting the term gives

( = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] \left( \frac{z}{a} \right)^{-n} )

which is equal to ( X(z/a) ).

The ROC is correspondingly scaled. If the original ROC is ( R_1 < |z| < R_2 ), then after scaling it becomes

( |a|R_1 < |z| < |a|R_2 ).

Example: Z-Transform of Cosine Sequence

Consider the sequence

( x[n] = \cos(\omega_0 n) u[n] )

Using Euler’s identity,

( \cos(\omega_0 n) = \frac{1}{2} \left( e^{j\omega_0 n} + e^{-j\omega_0 n} \right) )

Thus,

( x[n] = \frac{1}{2} e^{j\omega_0 n} u[n] + \frac{1}{2} e^{-j\omega_0 n} u[n] )

Now apply the Z-transform to each term separately.

We know that

( Z\{a^n u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - a}, \quad |z| > |a| )

For the first term, ( a = e^{j\omega_0} ):

( Z\{e^{j\omega_0 n} u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - e^{j\omega_0}} )

For the second term, ( a = e^{-j\omega_0} ):

( Z\{e^{-j\omega_0 n} u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - e^{-j\omega_0}} )

Therefore,

( X(z) = \frac{1}{2} \frac{z}{z - e^{j\omega_0}} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{z}{z - e^{-j\omega_0}} )

Combining the two fractions leads to a real-coefficient rational expression:

( X(z) = \frac{z(z - \cos(\omega_0))}{z^2 - 2z \cos(\omega_0) + 1} )

Poles and ROC

The poles occur at

( z = e^{j\omega_0} ) and ( z = e^{-j\omega_0} )

Since both poles lie on the unit circle ( |z| = 1 ), and the sequence is right-sided due to multiplication by ( u[n] ), the ROC is

( |z| > 1 )

Thus, the Z-transform exists outside the unit circle.

Conclusion

This page demonstrates how exponential modulation affects the Z-transform and how trigonometric sequences can be handled using Euler’s identity. The example shows that sinusoidal sequences correspond to complex-conjugate pole pairs located on the unit circle, and the ROC depends on whether the sequence is right-sided or left-sided.

pages.text:
Topic: Z-Transform of Damped Sinusoidal Sequence

This page extends the previous discussion by analyzing the Z-transform of a damped cosine sequence of the form

( x[n] = a^n \cos(\omega_0 n) u[n] )

where ( a ) is a real constant and ( u[n] ) is the unit step sequence.

Step 1: Express the Cosine Using Euler’s Identity

Using Euler’s formula,

( \cos(\omega_0 n) = \frac{1}{2} \left( e^{j\omega_0 n} + e^{-j\omega_0 n} \right) )

Substituting into the signal expression gives

( x[n] = \frac{1}{2} a^n e^{j\omega_0 n} u[n] + \frac{1}{2} a^n e^{-j\omega_0 n} u[n] )

This can be written as

( x[n] = \frac{1}{2} (a e^{j\omega_0})^n u[n] + \frac{1}{2} (a e^{-j\omega_0})^n u[n] )

Step 2: Apply the Z-Transform

Using the standard result

( Z\{b^n u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - b}, \quad |z| > |b| )

For the first term, ( b = a e^{j\omega_0} ):

( Z\{(a e^{j\omega_0})^n u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - a e^{j\omega_0}} )

For the second term, ( b = a e^{-j\omega_0} ):

( Z\{(a e^{-j\omega_0})^n u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - a e^{-j\omega_0}} )

Thus,

( X(z) = \frac{1}{2} \frac{z}{z - a e^{j\omega_0}} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{z}{z - a e^{-j\omega_0}} )

Step 3: Combine the Terms

Combining the two fractions gives a rational expression with real coefficients:

( X(z) = \frac{z (z - a \cos(\omega_0))}{z^2 - 2a z \cos(\omega_0) + a^2} )

Pole Locations

The denominator becomes zero at

( z = a e^{j\omega_0} ) and ( z = a e^{-j\omega_0} )

These are complex conjugate poles with magnitude ( |z| = |a| ). They lie on a circle of radius ( |a| ) in the z-plane.

Region of Convergence

Since the sequence is multiplied by ( u[n] ), it is right-sided. Therefore, the ROC is

( |z| > |a| )

This means the Z-transform converges outside the circle of radius ( |a| ).

Special Case

If ( a = 1 ), the sequence becomes a pure cosine multiplied by ( u[n] ). The poles lie on the unit circle, and the ROC becomes

( |z| > 1 )

Conclusion

This page demonstrates that damped sinusoidal sequences produce complex conjugate pole pairs whose radius equals the damping factor ( |a| ). The ROC depends on whether the sequence is right-sided or left-sided. For right-sided damped sinusoids, the ROC lies outside the circle determined by the pole magnitude.

Topic: Two-Sided Exponential Sequence and Region of Convergence

This page analyzes the Z-transform of a two-sided exponential sequence and determines its Region of Convergence (ROC). It highlights how the ROC differs from purely right-sided or left-sided signals.

Consider a sequence defined as

( x[n] = a^n )

for all integer values of ( n ). This sequence extends infinitely in both positive and negative directions, making it a two-sided sequence.

Z-Transform of Two-Sided Exponential

The Z-transform is defined as

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} a^n z^{-n} )

This summation can be separated into two parts:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a^n z^{-n} + \sum_{n=-\infty}^{-1} a^n z^{-n} )

First part (for n >= 0):

( \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (a z^{-1})^n )

This converges when

( |a z^{-1}| < 1 )

which implies

( |z| > |a| )

Second part (for n <= -1):

Let ( m = -n ). Then

( \sum_{n=-\infty}^{-1} a^n z^{-n} = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} a^{-m} z^{m} )

This becomes

( \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} (z/a)^m )

This geometric series converges when

( |z/a| < 1 )

which implies

( |z| < |a| )

Region of Convergence

For the total Z-transform to exist, both parts must converge simultaneously. Therefore, both conditions must be satisfied:

( |z| > |a| ) and ( |z| < |a| )

These conditions cannot be satisfied at the same time unless the inequality is strict between two different radii. Therefore, for a two-sided exponential sequence, the ROC is of the form

( R_1 < |z| < R_2 )

In this particular case, no valid ROC exists unless additional constraints are imposed. This shows that a purely two-sided exponential sequence does not have a valid Z-transform unless restricted.

Pole Behavior

If expressed in rational form, the Z-transform contains poles at ( z = a ) and possibly at ( z = 0 ). The ROC must exclude these poles and lie between them.

Brief Explanation

This page demonstrates that unlike right-sided sequences, two-sided sequences require convergence in both directions. As a result, the ROC becomes a ring-shaped region in the z-plane rather than a region extending outward or inward. The example illustrates that convergence conditions from positive and negative indices must both be satisfied, which restricts the possible ROC.

Topic: Practical Applications of the Z-Transform

This page introduces practical applications of the Z-transform in discrete-time signal processing and system analysis. It discusses convolution, system analysis using poles and zeros, solving difference equations, time reversal, and applications in control systems.

Convolution Property

If two discrete-time sequences ( x[n] ) and ( h[n] ) are convolved in time domain:

( y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k] h[n-k] )

then their Z-transforms satisfy

( Y(z) = X(z) H(z) )

This property simplifies convolution, since multiplication in the Z-domain replaces time-domain convolution.

Poles and Zeros

For a rational Z-transform

( H(z) = \frac{N(z)}{D(z)} )

The roots of ( N(z) ) are called zeros and the roots of ( D(z) ) are called poles.

Pole and zero locations determine system behavior, stability, and frequency response.

Solving Difference Equations

A linear constant-coefficient difference equation of the form

( y[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k x[n-k] - \sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k y[n-k] )

can be solved using the Z-transform.

Taking the Z-transform of both sides gives

( Y(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k z^{-k} X(z) - \sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k z^{-k} Y(z) )

Rearranging,

( Y(z) \left( 1 + \sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k z^{-k} \right) = X(z) \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k z^{-k} )

Thus, the transfer function becomes

( H(z) = \frac{Y(z)}{X(z)} = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k z^{-k}}{1 + \sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k z^{-k}} )

Time Reversal Property

If ( x[n] \xleftrightarrow{Z} X(z) ), then the time-reversed sequence ( x[-n] ) has Z-transform

( X(z^{-1}) )

The ROC is inverted accordingly.

Applications in Systems and Control

The Z-transform is widely used in digital control systems and signal processing for system design and analysis. It allows engineers to:

1. Analyze stability using pole locations.
2. Convert difference equations into algebraic equations.
3. Study system response using transfer functions.

Stability Condition

For causal systems, stability requires that all poles lie inside the unit circle, meaning

( |z| < 1 )

If the unit circle lies within the ROC, the system is stable and its Fourier transform exists.

Brief Explanation

This page highlights how the Z-transform converts convolution into multiplication, transforms difference equations into algebraic forms, and provides insight into system stability through pole-zero analysis. It demonstrates why specifying poles, zeros, and ROC is essential in practical signal and control system applications.

Topic: Inverse Z-Transform Using Partial Fraction Expansion

This page introduces a systematic method for computing the inverse Z-transform of a rational function using algebraic techniques rather than direct property matching. The focus is on expressing a given Z-domain function in a form suitable for inversion and determining the corresponding time-domain sequence along with its Region of Convergence (ROC).

Consider a rational Z-transform of the form

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - 3z^{-1}} )

Step 1: Express in Standard Form

To work with pole locations clearly, multiply numerator and denominator by ( z ) to eliminate negative powers:

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - 3} )

This shows that the function has a single pole at

( z = 3 )

Step 2: Identify the Type of Sequence from ROC

The time-domain signal corresponding to this transform depends entirely on the specified ROC.

If the ROC is

( |z| > 3 )

then the sequence is right-sided. Using the standard pair

( Z\{a^n u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - a}, \quad |z| > |a| )

we obtain

( x[n] = 3^n u[n] )

If instead the ROC is

( |z| < 3 )

then the sequence is left-sided. In that case, the inverse transform becomes

( x[n] = -3^n u[-n-1] )

This demonstrates that the same algebraic expression in the Z-domain can correspond to two different time-domain signals depending on the ROC.

Method Without Direct Property Matching

The page also outlines a procedural method for inverse Z-transform when direct matching is not obvious.

Suppose we have a rational function of the form

( X(z) = \frac{z}{(z - a)(z - b)} )

Step 1: Perform partial fraction expansion:

( X(z) = \frac{A}{z - a} + \frac{B}{z - b} )

Step 2: Solve for constants ( A ) and ( B ) by equating coefficients.

Step 3: Rewrite each term in the standard form

( \frac{z}{z - a} )

so that known inverse Z-transform pairs can be applied.

Step 4: Apply inverse Z-transform using

( Z^{-1} \left\{ \frac{z}{z - a} \right\} = a^n u[n], \quad |z| > |a| )

or the left-sided equivalent depending on the ROC.

Example Structure

If

( X(z) = \frac{z}{(z - 2)(z - 5)} )

then poles are at

( z = 2 ) and ( z = 5 )

If the ROC is

( |z| > 5 )

then the signal is right-sided and consists of a linear combination of ( 2^n u[n] ) and ( 5^n u[n] ).

If the ROC is

( 2 < |z| < 5 )

then the sequence is two-sided: one exponential is right-sided and the other left-sided.

If the ROC is

( |z| < 2 )

then the sequence is left-sided.

Conceptual Understanding

This page emphasizes that the inverse Z-transform requires two components:

1. The algebraic expression ( X(z) )
2. The Region of Convergence

Without the ROC, the inverse is not unique. Partial fraction expansion is a powerful algebraic method that reduces complicated rational functions into sums of simpler standard forms that can be inverted using known transform pairs.

Thus, the procedure for inverse Z-transform is:

1. Express the function in rational form.
2. Identify poles.
3. Determine the ROC.
4. Perform partial fraction expansion.
5. Apply known inverse transform pairs according to the ROC.

This method forms the foundation for solving discrete-time system responses and difference equations using the Z-transform.

Topic: Inverse Z-Transform of Left-Sided Sequences Using Time Reversal

This page focuses on computing the inverse Z-transform of left-sided sequences using the time-reversal property. It emphasizes how signals of the form ( a^n u[-n-1] ) are handled and how their Region of Convergence (ROC) differs from right-sided signals.

Left-Sided Exponential Sequence

Consider the sequence

( x[n] = a^n u[-n-1] )

This sequence is nonzero only for ( n <= -1 ). Therefore, it is left-sided (anti-causal).

Step 1: Compute the Z-Transform Directly

Using the definition

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} )

Since the sequence exists only for ( n <= -1 ), we write

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{-1} a^n z^{-n} )

Let ( m = -n ). Then when ( n = -1 ), ( m = 1 ), and as ( n -> -\infty ), ( m -> \infty ).

Thus, the summation becomes

( X(z) = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} a^{-m} z^{m} )

This can be written as

( X(z) = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{z}{a} \right)^m )

This is a geometric series with ratio ( r = z/a ).

Step 2: Convergence Condition

A geometric series converges when

( |r| < 1 )

Thus,

( \left| \frac{z}{a} \right| < 1 )

which implies

( |z| < |a| )

Therefore, the ROC is

( |z| < |a| )

Step 3: Evaluate the Sum

Using the geometric series formula

( \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} r^m = \frac{r}{1 - r}, \quad |r| < 1 )

we obtain

( X(z) = \frac{\frac{z}{a}}{1 - \frac{z}{a}} )

Simplifying,

( X(z) = \frac{z}{a - z} )

Multiplying numerator and denominator by ( -1 ) gives

( X(z) = \frac{-z}{z - a} )

Thus,

( Z\{a^n u[-n-1]\} = \frac{-z}{z - a}, \quad |z| < |a| )

Time-Reversal Property

If

( x[n] \xleftrightarrow{Z} X(z) )

then the time-reversed sequence

( x[-n] )

has Z-transform

( X(z^{-1}) )

The ROC is inverted accordingly.

This property allows left-sided signals to be derived from right-sided ones by replacing ( z ) with ( z^{-1} ) and adjusting the ROC.

Conceptual Interpretation

The key idea demonstrated on this page is that right-sided and left-sided exponentials produce similar algebraic forms but differ in sign and ROC.

For right-sided sequence:

( Z\{a^n u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - a}, \quad |z| > |a| )

For left-sided sequence:

( Z\{a^n u[-n-1]\} = \frac{-z}{z - a}, \quad |z| < |a| )

Thus, the ROC determines whether the exponential grows toward positive infinity (right-sided) or toward negative infinity (left-sided).

This page reinforces that inverse Z-transform problems must always specify the ROC, since the same algebraic expression can represent two different sequences depending on whether the ROC lies inside or outside the pole.

Topic: Z-Transform of n a^n u[n] and Differentiation Property

This page derives the Z-transform of a sequence of the form ( x[n] = n a^n u[n] ) using the differentiation property of the Z-transform. The derivation is systematic and shows how multiplying a sequence by ( n ) in time domain corresponds to differentiation in the Z-domain.

Step 1: Start from Known Transform Pair

We begin with the standard result for a right-sided exponential sequence:

( Z\{a^n u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - a}, \quad |z| > |a| )

Let

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} )

Step 2: Use the Differentiation Property

The differentiation property of the Z-transform states that

( Z\{n x[n]\} = -z \frac{d}{dz} X(z) )

This property allows us to compute the transform of sequences multiplied by ( n ) without recomputing the infinite sum.

Step 3: Apply the Property

Since

( x[n] = a^n u[n] )

we want

( Z\{n a^n u[n]\} )

Using the property,

( Z\{n a^n u[n]\} = -z \frac{d}{dz} \left( \frac{z}{z - a} \right) )

Step 4: Compute the Derivative

Let

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} )

Differentiate with respect to ( z ) using the quotient rule.

First write:

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} )

The derivative is

( \frac{d}{dz} \left( \frac{z}{z - a} \right) = \frac{(z - a)(1) - z(1)}{(z - a)^2} )

Simplifying the numerator:

( (z - a) - z = -a )

Thus,

( \frac{d}{dz} \left( \frac{z}{z - a} \right) = \frac{-a}{(z - a)^2} )

Step 5: Multiply by ( -z )

Using the differentiation property:

( Z\{n a^n u[n]\} = -z \cdot \frac{-a}{(z - a)^2} )

Simplifying:

( Z\{n a^n u[n]\} = \frac{a z}{(z - a)^2} )

Region of Convergence

The ROC remains the same as the original sequence because multiplication by ( n ) does not change convergence behavior for right-sided sequences. Therefore,

( |z| > |a| )

Final Result

( Z\{n a^n u[n]\} = \frac{a z}{(z - a)^2}, \quad |z| > |a| )

Conceptual Interpretation

Multiplying a time-domain sequence by ( n ) increases the order of the pole in the Z-domain. Originally, ( a^n u[n] ) has a simple pole at ( z = a ). After multiplication by ( n ), the transform has a double pole at ( z = a ).

This illustrates an important principle:

Time-domain multiplication by ( n ) corresponds to differentiation in the Z-domain and increases pole multiplicity.

This page establishes a powerful technique for computing inverse and forward Z-transforms of sequences involving polynomial factors multiplied by exponentials.

Topic: Properties of the Z-Transform – Linearity, Shifting, and Convolution

This page summarizes important operational properties of the Z-transform and explains how these properties affect the Region of Convergence (ROC). It also outlines a structured approach for solving problems in the Z-domain.

Linearity Property

If two sequences ( x_1[n] ) and ( x_2[n] ) have Z-transforms ( X_1(z) ) and ( X_2(z) ), then

( Z\{ a x_1[n] + b x_2[n] \} = a X_1(z) + b X_2(z) )

where ( a ) and ( b ) are constants.

The ROC of the resulting transform is at least the intersection of the individual ROCs. This means the combined transform converges only in the region where both original transforms converge.

Time-Shifting Property

If

( x[n] \xleftrightarrow{Z} X(z) )

then a time-shifted sequence

( x[n - k] )

has Z-transform

( Z\{x[n - k]\} = z^{-k} X(z) )

The ROC remains the same except possibly at ( z = 0 ) or ( z = \infty ), depending on the sign of ( k ).

For example:

If ( x[n] ) is right-sided and we delay it by ( k > 0 ), the ROC is unchanged.

If we advance the sequence, additional restrictions at ( z = 0 ) may appear.

Convolution Property

If

( y[n] = x_1[n] * x_2[n] )

where

( y[n] = \sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty} x_1[m] x_2[n - m] )

then

( Y(z) = X_1(z) X_2(z) )

The ROC of the product includes at least the intersection of the two individual ROCs, but poles introduced by multiplication must be excluded.

Multiplication by n in Time Domain

If

( x[n] \xleftrightarrow{Z} X(z) )

then

( Z\{ n x[n] \} = -z \frac{d}{dz} X(z) )

This property increases the order of poles in the Z-domain.

Summary of Problem-Solving Steps in Z-Transform

The page outlines a general method for solving problems:

1. Convert the time-domain sequence into the Z-domain using known transform pairs.
2. Apply algebraic operations such as multiplication, addition, or shifting.
3. Determine the ROC by analyzing pole locations and signal causality.
4. If required, perform inverse Z-transform using partial fraction expansion.

Key Observations About ROC

The ROC:

1. Does not include poles.
2. Is determined by the nature of the sequence (right-sided, left-sided, or two-sided).
3. May change under shifting operations.
4. Is at least the intersection region under addition or convolution.

Conceptual Understanding

This page consolidates the operational rules of the Z-transform. It shows that most time-domain operations correspond to simple algebraic manipulations in the Z-domain. However, the ROC must always be analyzed separately, because it determines convergence, stability, and uniqueness of the inverse transform.

Thus, both the algebraic expression ( X(z) ) and the ROC together completely describe the discrete-time signal.

Topic: Convolution, Sequence Reversal, and Z-Domain Representation

This page continues the discussion of convolution and related sequence operations in the Z-domain. It emphasizes how time-domain convolution, reversal, and exponential multiplication correspond to algebraic operations in the Z-domain.

Convolution in Time Domain

For two discrete-time sequences ( x_1[n] ) and ( x_2[n] ), convolution is defined as

( y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x_1[k] x_2[n-k] )

Taking the Z-transform of both sides gives

( Y(z) = X_1(z) X_2(z) )

Thus, convolution in time domain becomes multiplication in the Z-domain. This property significantly simplifies system analysis because cascading systems corresponds to multiplying their transfer functions.

Effect of Sequence Reversal

If

( x[n] \xleftrightarrow{Z} X(z) )

then the time-reversed sequence

( x[-n] )

has Z-transform

( X(z^{-1}) )

The Region of Convergence (ROC) is inverted with respect to the unit circle. That is, if the original ROC is

( R_1 < |z| < R_2 )

then after reversal it becomes

( \frac{1}{R_2} < |z| < \frac{1}{R_1} )

This property is important when analyzing systems that involve reflection or backward indexing.

Multiplication by Exponential Sequence

If a sequence is multiplied by ( a^n ), that is,

( y[n] = a^n x[n] )

then the Z-transform becomes

( Y(z) = X\left( \frac{z}{a} \right) )

The ROC scales accordingly by a factor of ( |a| ). If the original ROC is

( R_1 < |z| < R_2 )

then the new ROC becomes

( |a|R_1 < |z| < |a|R_2 )

Combined Operations

The page outlines that when multiple operations such as shifting, reversal, multiplication, and convolution are combined, the procedure should be:

1. Express each sequence in Z-domain using known transform pairs.
2. Apply algebraic operations corresponding to time-domain manipulations.
3. Determine the new ROC by considering pole locations and transformation effects.

Important Observations

1. Convolution corresponds to multiplication of transforms.
2. Reversal corresponds to replacing ( z ) with ( z^{-1} ).
3. Multiplication by ( a^n ) corresponds to scaling the argument of ( X(z) ).
4. ROC must be recomputed after each operation.

Conceptual Understanding

This page reinforces the idea that the Z-transform provides a powerful algebraic framework for handling complex time-domain operations. Instead of directly computing convolution sums or shifted expressions, one can work in the Z-domain, perform algebraic manipulation, and then apply the inverse transform. However, careful attention must always be given to the ROC, as it determines convergence and the correct interpretation of the sequence.

Thus, the Z-transform not only simplifies computations but also provides structural insight into discrete-time system behavior.

Topic: Correlation, Auto-Correlation, and Power Spectral Density Using Z-Transform

This page introduces the concept of correlation in discrete-time signals and explains its relationship with the Z-transform. It also connects auto-correlation with power spectral density, which is a fundamental concept in signal analysis.

Cross-Correlation Definition

For two discrete-time sequences ( x[n] ) and ( y[n] ), the cross-correlation is defined as

( r_{xy}[m] = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] y[n - m] )

This expression resembles convolution, but instead of reversing one signal explicitly, correlation measures similarity between two sequences as one is shifted relative to the other.

Relationship Between Correlation and Convolution

Correlation can be expressed in terms of convolution. If we define

( y_r[n] = y[-n] )

then cross-correlation becomes

( r_{xy}[m] = x[n] * y_r[n] )

Thus, correlation is equivalent to convolution with a time-reversed version of one signal.

Z-Transform of Cross-Correlation

If

( x[n] \xleftrightarrow{Z} X(z) )

and

( y[n] \xleftrightarrow{Z} Y(z) )

then using the time-reversal property

( y[-n] \xleftrightarrow{Z} Y(z^{-1}) )

Since convolution corresponds to multiplication in the Z-domain,

( R_{xy}(z) = X(z) Y(z^{-1}) )

This result shows that correlation in time domain corresponds to multiplication of one transform with the reversed transform of the other.

Auto-Correlation

Auto-correlation is a special case of cross-correlation where a sequence is correlated with itself:

( r_{xx}[m] = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] x[n - m] )

In the Z-domain, this becomes

( R_{xx}(z) = X(z) X(z^{-1}) )

This expression is always real and symmetric for real sequences.

Power Spectral Density

The page connects auto-correlation with power spectral density. The power spectral density (PSD) of a discrete-time signal is defined as the Fourier transform of its auto-correlation sequence.

If

( R_{xx}(e^{j\omega}) )

is the Fourier transform of the auto-correlation, then

( S_{xx}(e^{j\omega}) = X(e^{j\omega}) X(e^{-j\omega}) )

Since

( X(e^{-j\omega}) = X^*(e^{j\omega}) )

for real sequences, the power spectral density becomes

( S_{xx}(e^{j\omega}) = |X(e^{j\omega})|^2 )

Thus, the power spectral density is equal to the magnitude squared of the Fourier transform.

Conceptual Understanding

This page highlights that:

1. Correlation measures similarity between signals.
2. Correlation can be computed using convolution with time reversal.
3. In the Z-domain, correlation corresponds to multiplication with a reversed transform.
4. Auto-correlation leads directly to power spectral density.
5. Power spectral density represents how signal power is distributed across frequency.

This establishes a strong link between time-domain similarity analysis and frequency-domain energy distribution using the Z-transform framework.

Topic: Initial Value Theorem of the Z-Transform

This page introduces and proves the Initial Value Theorem (IVT) for the Z-transform. The theorem provides a direct way to compute the first sample of a discrete-time sequence from its Z-transform without performing the full inverse transform.

Statement of the Initial Value Theorem

If ( x[n] ) is a causal sequence (that is, ( x[n] = 0 ) for ( n < 0 )), and its Z-transform is ( X(z) ), then the initial value is given by

( x[0] = \lim_{z \to \infty} X(z) )

This result holds provided the limit exists.

Proof of the Theorem

Start from the definition of the Z-transform for a causal sequence:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} )

Expanding the summation explicitly,

( X(z) = x[0] + x[1] z^{-1} + x[2] z^{-2} + x[3] z^{-3} + \dots )

Now take the limit as ( z \to \infty ).

As ( z \to \infty ), all terms containing negative powers of ( z ) approach zero because

( z^{-n} \to 0 \quad \text{for } n \ge 1 )

Thus,

( \lim_{z \to \infty} X(z) = x[0] )

This proves the Initial Value Theorem.

Interpretation

The reason this theorem works is that as ( z ) becomes very large, the terms involving ( z^{-1}, z^{-2}, \dots ) vanish, leaving only the constant term ( x[0] ).

Example

Suppose

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} )

Then

( \lim_{z \to \infty} \frac{z}{z - a} = 1 )

Thus,

( x[0] = 1 )

If the corresponding time-domain sequence is ( x[n] = a^n u[n] ), then indeed

( x[0] = a^0 = 1 )

which confirms the theorem.

Important Condition

The theorem applies only to causal sequences. If the sequence is not causal, the expansion used in the proof is not valid in the same form.

Conceptual Understanding

The Initial Value Theorem provides a quick method to determine the first value of a discrete-time signal directly from its Z-transform. Instead of performing partial fraction expansion or inverse transformation, one simply evaluates the limit as ( z \to \infty ).

This theorem is particularly useful when verifying solutions of difference equations or checking system responses.

Thus, the key result of this page is:

( x[0] = \lim_{z \to \infty} X(z) )

for causal sequences.

pages.text:
Topic: Final Value Theorem of the Z-Transform

This page introduces the Final Value Theorem (FVT) for the Z-transform. The theorem provides a direct method to compute the steady-state value of a discrete-time sequence without explicitly computing the inverse Z-transform.

Statement of the Final Value Theorem

If ( x[n] ) is a causal sequence and all poles of ( (1 - z^{-1}) X(z) ) lie inside the unit circle except possibly a simple pole at ( z = 1 ), then the final value of the sequence is given by

( \lim_{n \to \infty} x[n] = \lim_{z \to 1} (1 - z^{-1}) X(z) )

This theorem determines the steady-state value of a sequence as ( n \to \infty ).

Derivation Outline

Start from the definition of the Z-transform of a causal sequence:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} )

Multiply both sides by ( 1 - z^{-1} ):

( (1 - z^{-1}) X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} - \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-(n+1)} )

Shift the index in the second summation:

( = x[0] + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (x[n] - x[n-1]) z^{-n} )

Now take the limit as ( z \to 1 ).

As ( z \to 1 ), the summation converges to

( \lim_{z \to 1} (1 - z^{-1}) X(z) = \lim_{n \to \infty} x[n] )

provided the sequence converges and the stability conditions are satisfied.

Example

Consider

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} )

which corresponds to ( x[n] = a^n u[n] ).

Applying the Final Value Theorem:

( \lim_{n \to \infty} x[n] = \lim_{z \to 1} (1 - z^{-1}) \frac{z}{z - a} )

First simplify ( 1 - z^{-1} ):

( 1 - z^{-1} = \frac{z - 1}{z} )

Thus,

( (1 - z^{-1}) X(z) = \frac{z - 1}{z} \cdot \frac{z}{z - a} )

Simplifying,

( = \frac{z - 1}{z - a} )

Now take the limit as ( z \to 1 ):

( \lim_{z \to 1} \frac{z - 1}{z - a} = \frac{0}{1 - a} = 0 )

Thus,

( \lim_{n \to \infty} a^n u[n] = 0 )

This result is valid when ( |a| < 1 ), ensuring stability and convergence.

Important Condition

The theorem is valid only if:

1. The sequence is causal.
2. All poles of ( (1 - z^{-1}) X(z) ) lie inside the unit circle.
3. There is at most a simple pole at ( z = 1 ).

If poles lie outside the unit circle, the sequence diverges and the final value does not exist.

Conceptual Understanding

The Final Value Theorem provides the steady-state value of a sequence directly from its Z-transform. Instead of computing the entire inverse transform, one evaluates a limit at ( z = 1 ).

The theorem is particularly useful in system analysis to determine steady-state response to inputs, especially in digital control systems.

Thus, the key result of this page is:

( \lim_{n \to \infty} x[n] = \lim_{z \to 1} (1 - z^{-1}) X(z) )

subject to stability conditions.

Topic: Stability, Unit Circle, and Partial Fraction Expansion

This page discusses the relationship between the Region of Convergence (ROC) and system stability. It also presents an example involving partial fraction expansion of a rational Z-transform and identification of poles.

Stability and the Unit Circle

For a discrete-time system to be stable, the unit circle defined by

( |z| = 1 )

must lie within the Region of Convergence (ROC) of the system function ( H(z) ).

If the ROC includes the unit circle, then the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform exists, and the system is BIBO stable.

Thus, stability condition:

The unit circle must be included in the ROC.

If the unit circle is not included in the ROC, the system is unstable.

Rational Z-Transform and Pole Analysis

Consider a rational Z-transform of the form

( X(z) = \frac{P(z)}{Q(z)} )

where ( Q(z) ) determines the pole locations.

The poles are obtained by solving

( Q(z) = 0 )

The ROC cannot include pole locations. Therefore, for stability of a causal system, all poles must lie strictly inside the unit circle.

Example: Polynomial in z^{-1}

Suppose a transform is given in terms of negative powers of ( z ) and is rewritten in standard rational form.

For example, assume

( X(z) = \frac{2z^2 - 4z + 1}{(z - 2)(z - 3)} )

Poles occur at

( z = 2 ) and ( z = 3 )

Since both poles lie outside the unit circle ( |z| > 1 ), a causal system with ROC

( |z| > 3 )

would not include the unit circle. Therefore, such a system would be unstable.

Partial Fraction Expansion

To compute the inverse Z-transform, express the rational function as

( X(z) = \frac{A}{z - 2} + \frac{B}{z - 3} )

Solve for constants ( A ) and ( B ) by equating coefficients.

Once decomposed, rewrite each term in the form

( \frac{z}{z - a} )

so that standard inverse Z-transform pairs can be applied.

Interpretation of Pole Locations

1. If all poles lie inside ( |z| < 1 ), the system is stable and causal.
2. If poles lie outside the unit circle and ROC is outside, the system is unstable.
3. If ROC is between poles, the system is two-sided.

Conceptual Summary

This page emphasizes that:

1. Stability depends on whether the unit circle lies inside the ROC.
2. Poles determine possible ROCs.
3. Partial fraction expansion is used to compute inverse transforms.
4. A rational function alone is not sufficient to determine stability; the ROC must be specified.

The key takeaway is that pole location relative to the unit circle determines system stability in discrete-time signal processing.

pages.text:
Topic: Absolute Summability, ROC, and Stability Conditions

This page discusses the relationship between the Region of Convergence (ROC), absolute summability, and stability of discrete-time systems. It emphasizes how convergence properties in the Z-domain determine whether a sequence is stable.

Absolute Summability

A discrete-time sequence ( x[n] ) is said to be absolutely summable if

( \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} |x[n]| < \infty )

Absolute summability is an important condition for stability. If the impulse response of a system is absolutely summable, then the system is BIBO stable.

Connection Between ROC and Absolute Summability

For a sequence to be absolutely summable, the unit circle

( |z| = 1 )

must lie inside the ROC of its Z-transform.

If the ROC includes the unit circle, then the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform exists, and the sequence is stable.

If the unit circle is not included in the ROC, the sequence is not absolutely summable and the system is unstable.

Pole and ROC Observations

1. The ROC cannot include poles.
2. The ROC is a circular region centered at the origin.
3. For right-sided sequences, the ROC is of the form ( |z| > R ).
4. For left-sided sequences, the ROC is of the form ( |z| < R ).
5. For two-sided sequences, the ROC is of the form ( R_1 < |z| < R_2 ).

Example: Exponential Sequence

Consider

( x[n] = a^n u[n] )

Its Z-transform is

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} )

with ROC

( |z| > |a| )

If ( |a| < 1 ), then the ROC includes the unit circle. Hence, the sequence is absolutely summable and stable.

If ( |a| > 1 ), then the ROC does not include the unit circle, and the sequence grows without bound. Therefore, it is unstable.

Geometric Interpretation in the Z-Plane

The ROC is always centered at the origin in the z-plane. Stability depends on whether the unit circle lies within this region. Pole locations determine the boundaries of the ROC.

Summary of Stability Conditions

1. For a causal system, stability requires all poles to lie strictly inside the unit circle.
2. The ROC must include the unit circle.
3. Absolute summability ensures BIBO stability.

Conceptual Understanding

This page reinforces that stability in discrete-time systems is directly tied to the ROC. The key test is whether the unit circle is included in the ROC. Pole positions determine the ROC boundaries, and therefore determine whether the system is stable or unstable.

Thus, stability analysis in the Z-domain reduces to examining pole locations relative to the unit circle.

Topic: ROC Conditions for Right-Sided Sequences and Stability Analysis

This page analyzes how the Region of Convergence (ROC) behaves for right-sided sequences and connects these conditions directly to stability and boundedness of signals.

Right-Sided Sequence and ROC

Consider a right-sided sequence ( x[n] ) such that

( x[n] = 0 \quad \text{for } n < 0 )

Its Z-transform is

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} )

For right-sided sequences, the ROC always has the form

( |z| > R )

where ( R ) is determined by the magnitude of the outermost pole.

If ( |z| = r ) is within the ROC, then any value of ( |z| > r ) will also lie in the ROC. Thus, the ROC extends outward to infinity.

Condition for Stability

For a system to be stable, its impulse response must be absolutely summable:

( \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |x[n]| < \infty )

This condition is satisfied if and only if the unit circle

( |z| = 1 )

lies inside the ROC.

Thus, for right-sided sequences:

If ( R < 1 ), then the ROC includes the unit circle and the system is stable.

If ( R > 1 ), then the ROC does not include the unit circle and the system is unstable.

Exponential Example

Consider

( x[n] = a^n u[n] )

The Z-transform is

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} )

with ROC

( |z| > |a| )

If ( |a| < 1 ), then the ROC includes ( |z| = 1 ). Therefore, the sequence decays and is absolutely summable.

If ( |a| > 1 ), then the ROC lies outside the unit circle, and the sequence grows exponentially. In this case, it is not absolutely summable and is unstable.

Boundedness Assumption

The page notes that if a sequence is bounded, meaning there exists a constant ( M ) such that

( |x[n]| \le M )

this does not necessarily imply absolute summability. Stability requires summability, not just boundedness.

Geometric Interpretation

In the z-plane, the ROC for a right-sided sequence is an exterior region outside a circle centered at the origin. Stability requires that this exterior region include the unit circle.

If the pole radius is less than 1, the ROC boundary lies inside the unit circle and the sequence decays.

If the pole radius exceeds 1, the ROC lies outside the unit circle and the sequence grows.

Final Observation

For right-sided sequences:

1. ROC is always of the form ( |z| > R ).
2. Stability requires ( R < 1 ).
3. Absolute summability ensures BIBO stability.
4. Pole magnitude determines whether the sequence grows or decays.

This page reinforces that for causal systems, stability analysis reduces to checking whether all poles lie inside the unit circle.

Topic: ROC for Different Types of Sequences and Definition of Poles and Zeros

This page discusses how the Region of Convergence (ROC) behaves for right-sided, left-sided, and two-sided sequences. It also formally defines poles and zeros of a Z-transform and explains their significance.

ROC for Right-Sided Sequences

For a right-sided sequence, that is, a sequence of the form

( x[n] = 0 \quad \text{for } n < N_0 )

its Z-transform has an ROC of the form

( |z| > R )

where ( R ) is determined by the magnitude of the outermost pole.

The ROC extends outward to infinity and is bounded internally by the pole of largest magnitude. The ROC does not include the pole itself.

ROC for Left-Sided Sequences

For a left-sided sequence, that is,

( x[n] = 0 \quad \text{for } n > N_0 )

its ROC has the form

( |z| < R )

where ( R ) corresponds to the pole of smallest magnitude.

In this case, the ROC extends inward toward the origin and is bounded externally by a pole.

ROC for Two-Sided Sequences

For two-sided sequences, which extend infinitely in both positive and negative directions, the ROC is an annular region:

( R_1 < |z| < R_2 )

Thus, the ROC is bounded by two poles. It lies between an inner pole and an outer pole.

Important Observations About ROC

1. The ROC is always a connected region.
2. The ROC cannot contain any poles.
3. The ROC is determined by the time-domain nature of the sequence.
4. The same algebraic expression may correspond to different signals depending on the ROC.

Definition of Poles

For a rational Z-transform

( X(z) = \frac{N(z)}{D(z)} )

where ( N(z) ) and ( D(z) ) are polynomials in ( z ),

poles are defined as the values of ( z ) that make the denominator zero:

( D(z) = 0 )

At a pole, the Z-transform becomes unbounded (infinite).

Definition of Zeros

Zeros are the values of ( z ) that make the numerator zero:

( N(z) = 0 )

At a zero, the Z-transform becomes zero.

Procedure to Find Poles and Zeros

1. Express ( X(z) ) in rational form.
2. Set the denominator equal to zero to find poles.
3. Set the numerator equal to zero to find zeros.

Conceptual Meaning

Poles determine the boundaries of the ROC and strongly influence system stability and time-domain behavior.

Zeros influence the frequency response and shape of the spectrum but do not directly determine the ROC boundaries.

Summary

This page formalizes the behavior of ROC for different sequence types and defines poles and zeros mathematically. The key takeaway is that poles determine ROC boundaries and stability, while zeros determine frequency shaping characteristics.

Topic: General Form of Rational Z-Transform and Trivial Poles/Zeros

This page discusses the general structure of a rational Z-transform and explains the concepts of trivial poles and trivial zeros. It also analyzes how the relative degrees of numerator and denominator polynomials affect pole-zero behavior.

General Rational Form

A general rational Z-transform can be written as

( X(z) = K \frac{(z - z_1)(z - z_2) \dots (z - z_M)}{(z - p_1)(z - p_2) \dots (z - p_N)} )

where:

1. ( z_1, z_2, \dots, z_M ) are zeros.
2. ( p_1, p_2, \dots, p_N ) are poles.
3. ( K ) is a constant gain factor.

Zeros are obtained by solving

( N(z) = 0 )

Poles are obtained by solving

( D(z) = 0 )

Trivial Zeros and Poles

When expressing the Z-transform in terms of negative powers of ( z ), additional zeros or poles may appear at the origin.

If the degree of the numerator polynomial is less than the degree of the denominator polynomial ( M < N ), then there are

( N - M )

trivial poles at ( z = 0 ).

If the degree of the numerator polynomial is greater than the denominator degree ( M > N ), then there are

( M - N )

trivial zeros at ( z = 0 ).

Case Analysis

Case 1: ( M < N )

The function is strictly proper. As ( z \to \infty ),

( X(z) \to 0 )

This implies the system has more poles than zeros, and trivial poles may exist at the origin.

Case 2: ( M = N )

The function is proper. As ( z \to \infty ),

( X(z) \to K )

The number of poles equals the number of zeros. No trivial pole or zero is introduced at infinity.

Case 3: ( M > N )

The function is improper. In this case, the transform may contain trivial zeros at the origin when rewritten in standard form.

Interpretation

Trivial poles at ( z = 0 ) correspond to factors of ( z^{-1} ) in the transform. These arise naturally when expressing transforms in terms of negative powers of ( z ).

Trivial zeros at ( z = 0 ) correspond to excess positive powers of ( z ) in the numerator.

Importance

Understanding trivial poles and zeros is important when:

1. Drawing pole-zero plots.
2. Determining system type.
3. Evaluating stability.
4. Performing inverse Z-transform.

Summary

This page formalizes the factorized representation of rational Z-transforms and clarifies how the difference between numerator and denominator degrees determines additional poles or zeros at the origin. Proper classification of these cases is essential for correct system analysis and interpretation in the Z-domain.

pages.text:
Topic: Improper Rational Functions and Pole-Zero Plot Interpretation

This page continues the discussion of rational Z-transforms by analyzing the case where the degree of the numerator is greater than the degree of the denominator. It also emphasizes the interpretation of pole-zero plots and geometric behavior in the z-plane.

Case: Improper Rational Function (M > N)

Consider a rational Z-transform of the form

( X(z) = K \frac{(z - z_1)(z - z_2) \dots (z - z_M)}{(z - p_1)(z - p_2) \dots (z - p_N)} )

If the degree of the numerator (M) is greater than the degree of the denominator (N), then the function is improper.

In such a case, the transform may be rewritten by performing polynomial division:

( X(z) = Q(z) + \frac{R(z)}{D(z)} )

where:

1. ( Q(z) ) is a polynomial term.
2. ( R(z) ) is a remainder polynomial whose degree is less than the denominator.

This decomposition separates the strictly proper part from the polynomial part.

Trivial Zeros at the Origin

When expressed in terms of negative powers of ( z ), an improper rational function introduces additional zeros at the origin. These arise due to excess powers of ( z ) in the numerator.

If ( M - N = k ), then there are ( k ) trivial zeros at ( z = 0 ).

Geometric Interpretation in the Z-Plane

In a pole-zero plot:

1. Poles are marked at locations where the denominator becomes zero.
2. Zeros are marked at locations where the numerator becomes zero.
3. Trivial zeros at ( z = 0 ) appear at the origin.

The behavior of ( X(z) ) depends on the relative position of poles and zeros.

Magnitude Behavior

The magnitude of ( X(z) ) tends to increase near poles and decrease near zeros. The closer a point in the z-plane is to a pole, the larger the magnitude of the transform.

Conversely, if the evaluation point is close to a zero, the magnitude decreases.

Example Structure

Suppose

( X(z) = \frac{z^2 + a z + b}{z - p} )

Since the numerator degree (2) is greater than the denominator degree (1), polynomial division must be performed before applying inverse Z-transform methods.

After division:

( X(z) = A z + B + \frac{C}{z - p} )

The polynomial part corresponds to impulses and shifted impulses in time domain.

Key Observations

1. Improper rational functions require polynomial division.
2. Excess numerator degree creates trivial zeros at the origin.
3. Pole-zero plots visually represent system structure.
4. Magnitude response depends on distance from poles and zeros.

Conceptual Understanding

This page emphasizes that when analyzing Z-transforms, degree comparison between numerator and denominator is crucial. Improper transforms must be reduced to proper form before inverse transformation. Additionally, pole-zero plots provide geometric insight into system behavior, stability, and frequency response.

Thus, both algebraic manipulation and geometric interpretation are essential tools in Z-domain analysis.

pages.text:
Topic: Inverse Z-Transform Using Pole-Zero Plot and Residue Method

This page discusses a second method for computing the inverse Z-transform using pole-zero analysis. It connects algebraic decomposition with geometric interpretation in the z-plane and emphasizes how residues at poles determine the time-domain sequence.

Pole-Zero Representation

A rational Z-transform can be written in factored form as

( X(z) = K \frac{(z - z_1)(z - z_2) \dots}{(z - p_1)(z - p_2) \dots} )

where ( p_i ) are poles and ( z_i ) are zeros.

The pole-zero plot visually represents these locations in the complex plane.

Second Method for Inverse Z-Transform

Instead of directly applying transform pairs, the inverse Z-transform can be computed using partial fraction expansion or residue evaluation at each pole.

Consider a simple rational function with distinct poles:

( X(z) = \frac{N(z)}{(z - p_1)(z - p_2)} )

We decompose it as

( X(z) = \frac{A_1}{z - p_1} + \frac{A_2}{z - p_2} )

To find coefficient ( A_1 ), multiply both sides by ( z - p_1 ) and evaluate at ( z = p_1 ):

( A_1 = \left. (z - p_1) X(z) \right|_{z = p_1} )

Similarly,

( A_2 = \left. (z - p_2) X(z) \right|_{z = p_2} )

This method is called the residue method.

Connection to Time-Domain Sequence

After decomposition, each term has the form

( \frac{A}{z - p} )

To convert into standard inverse transform form, multiply numerator and denominator by ( z ):

( \frac{A}{z - p} = \frac{A}{z} \cdot \frac{z}{z - p} )

Using the standard pair

( Z^{-1} \left\{ \frac{z}{z - p} \right\} = p^n u[n], \quad |z| > |p| )

Thus, the inverse transform becomes

( x[n] = A p^n u[n] )

if the ROC indicates a right-sided sequence.

If the ROC is inside the pole magnitude, the sequence becomes left-sided.

Geometric Interpretation

In the pole-zero plot:

1. Each pole contributes an exponential term ( p^n ).
2. The residue at the pole determines the amplitude.
3. The ROC determines whether the exponential is right-sided or left-sided.

Example Structure

If

( X(z) = \frac{1}{(z - p_1)(z - p_2)} )

then the time-domain sequence is a linear combination of

( p_1^n u[n] ) and ( p_2^n u[n] )

for a right-sided ROC.

Key Insight

The inverse Z-transform can be computed either:

1. Using standard transform pairs.
2. Using partial fraction expansion.
3. Using residue evaluation directly at poles.

The pole-zero plot helps visualize how each pole contributes an exponential component to the sequence.

Conceptual Summary

This page emphasizes that poles determine the fundamental exponential components of the time-domain signal. The residue method provides a systematic way to extract these components directly from the algebraic form of ( X(z) ). The ROC determines whether these exponentials grow toward positive or negative infinity in time.

Thus, inverse Z-transform computation is fundamentally linked to pole locations and their residues in the z-plane.

Topic: Z-Transform of Sinusoidal Sequences and Frequency Response Interpretation

This page analyzes the Z-transform of sinusoidal sequences and connects the result to frequency-domain interpretation. The derivation focuses on cosine sequences and how their pole locations relate to oscillatory behavior.

Z-Transform of Cosine Sequence

Consider the sequence

( x[n] = \cos(\omega_0 n) u[n] )

Using Euler’s identity,

( \cos(\omega_0 n) = \frac{1}{2} \left( e^{j\omega_0 n} + e^{-j\omega_0 n} \right) )

Thus,

( x[n] = \frac{1}{2} e^{j\omega_0 n} u[n] + \frac{1}{2} e^{-j\omega_0 n} u[n] )

Apply the standard Z-transform result for exponentials:

( Z\{a^n u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - a}, \quad |z| > |a| )

For ( a = e^{j\omega_0} ),

( Z\{e^{j\omega_0 n} u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - e^{j\omega_0}} )

For ( a = e^{-j\omega_0} ),

( Z\{e^{-j\omega_0 n} u[n]\} = \frac{z}{z - e^{-j\omega_0}} )

Therefore,

( X(z) = \frac{1}{2} \frac{z}{z - e^{j\omega_0}} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{z}{z - e^{-j\omega_0}} )

Combine the two fractions to obtain a real-coefficient expression:

( X(z) = \frac{z (z - \cos(\omega_0))}{z^2 - 2z \cos(\omega_0) + 1} )

Pole Locations

The denominator becomes zero at

( z = e^{j\omega_0} ) and ( z = e^{-j\omega_0} )

These are complex conjugate poles located on the unit circle, since

( |e^{j\omega_0}| = 1 )

Region of Convergence

Because the sequence is right-sided due to multiplication by ( u[n] ), the ROC is

( |z| > 1 )

The ROC lies outside the unit circle and does not include the poles.

Frequency Response Interpretation

To obtain the frequency response, evaluate the Z-transform on the unit circle:

( z = e^{j\omega} )

Thus,

( X(e^{j\omega}) )

represents the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform.

The magnitude response shows peaks near the pole angles ( \pm \omega_0 ). The closer the poles are to the unit circle, the sharper the frequency response peak.

Key Observations

1. Sinusoidal sequences produce complex conjugate pole pairs.
2. Pole angles determine oscillation frequency.
3. Pole magnitude determines exponential growth or decay.
4. Poles on the unit circle correspond to sustained oscillations.

Conceptual Understanding

This page highlights the deep connection between pole location and time-domain behavior. A pole located at

( z = r e^{j\omega_0} )

corresponds to a sequence of the form

( r^n \cos(\omega_0 n) )

If ( r < 1 ), the oscillation decays.
If ( r = 1 ), the oscillation is sustained.
If ( r > 1 ), the oscillation grows.

Thus, sinusoidal signals in discrete time are directly represented by complex conjugate pole pairs in the Z-domain, and their frequency characteristics are determined by the pole angle.

pages.text:
Topic: Solving Difference Equations Using Z-Transform and Natural Response

This page discusses how to solve linear constant-coefficient difference equations using the Z-transform. It separates the total response into natural (homogeneous) and forced (particular) components and connects pole locations to system behavior.

General Linear Difference Equation

Consider a second-order linear difference equation of the form

( y[n] - a y[n-1] = x[n] )

Taking the Z-transform of both sides (assuming zero initial conditions):

( Y(z) - a z^{-1} Y(z) = X(z) )

Factor ( Y(z) ):

( Y(z) (1 - a z^{-1}) = X(z) )

Thus, the transfer function is

( H(z) = \frac{Y(z)}{X(z)} = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} )

Multiply numerator and denominator by ( z ) to obtain

( H(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} )

Pole Location and ROC

The system has a pole at

( z = a )

If the system is causal, the ROC is

( |z| > |a| )

If ( |a| < 1 ), the pole lies inside the unit circle and the system is stable.

Natural Response

The natural response corresponds to solving the homogeneous equation:

( y[n] - a y[n-1] = 0 )

Assume a solution of the form

( y[n] = C r^n )

Substituting gives

( r^n - a r^{n-1} = 0 )

Divide by ( r^{n-1} ):

( r - a = 0 )

Thus,

( r = a )

Therefore, the natural response is

( y_h[n] = C a^n )

This matches the pole location interpretation: each pole corresponds to an exponential term in the time domain.

Forced Response

If the input is a unit step

( x[n] = u[n] )

then

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - 1} )

The total output becomes

( Y(z) = H(z) X(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} \cdot \frac{z}{z - 1} )

Simplify:

( Y(z) = \frac{z^2}{(z - a)(z - 1)} )

Perform partial fraction expansion:

( Y(z) = \frac{A}{z - a} + \frac{B}{z - 1} )

Solve for constants ( A ) and ( B ).

The time-domain response becomes

( y[n] = A a^n u[n] + B (1)^n u[n] )

Thus, the output consists of:

1. A natural response term ( a^n ).
2. A forced response term corresponding to the input pole at ( z = 1 ).

Key Insight

The complete solution of a difference equation consists of:

( y[n] = y_h[n] + y_p[n] )

where:

1. ( y_h[n] ) is determined by system poles.
2. ( y_p[n] ) is determined by input poles.

Stability Interpretation

If ( |a| < 1 ), the natural response decays.
If ( |a| = 1 ), oscillations persist.
If ( |a| > 1 ), the natural response grows and the system is unstable.

Conceptual Summary

This page connects three viewpoints:

1. Algebraic solution using Z-transform.
2. Difference equation solution in time domain.
3. Pole-based interpretation of system behavior.

Each pole of the system corresponds to an exponential component in the natural response. The input introduces additional poles that shape the forced response. Stability depends entirely on whether system poles lie inside the unit circle.

Thus, solving difference equations using the Z-transform reduces to algebraic manipulation followed by inverse transformation guided by pole locations.

Topic: System Function, Convolution, and Determining Output Using Z-Transform

This page discusses how to determine the output of a discrete-time Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) system using its system function. It connects convolution, transfer function representation, and algebraic manipulation in the Z-domain.

System Function Definition

For an LTI discrete-time system, the system function (transfer function) is defined as

( H(z) = \frac{Y(z)}{X(z)} )

where:

1. ( X(z) ) is the Z-transform of the input sequence ( x[n] ).
2. ( Y(z) ) is the Z-transform of the output sequence ( y[n] ).

The impulse response ( h[n] ) is related to the system function by

( H(z) = Z\{h[n]\} )

Output via Convolution

In the time domain, the output of an LTI system is given by convolution:

( y[n] = x[n] * h[n] )

where

( y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k] h[n-k] )

In the Z-domain, convolution becomes multiplication:

( Y(z) = X(z) H(z) )

Thus, the output can be computed by:

1. Finding ( X(z) ) from the input.
2. Using the given ( H(z) ).
3. Multiplying to obtain ( Y(z) ).
4. Taking the inverse Z-transform to obtain ( y[n] ).

Goal: Finding y[n]

If ( H(z) ) and ( X(z) ) are known, then

( Y(z) = H(z) X(z) )

After simplification, apply partial fraction expansion if necessary and use known transform pairs to compute ( y[n] ).

Goal: Finding h[n]

If the system function ( H(z) ) is given and the goal is to find the impulse response ( h[n] ), compute the inverse Z-transform of ( H(z) ).

Goal: Finding x[n]

If ( Y(z) ) and ( H(z) ) are given, then

( X(z) = \frac{Y(z)}{H(z)} )

provided ( H(z) ) is nonzero. Then compute the inverse Z-transform to obtain ( x[n] ).

Difference Equation Interpretation

If the system is described by a difference equation of the form

( y[n] + a_1 y[n-1] + a_2 y[n-2] = b_0 x[n] + b_1 x[n-1] )

Taking the Z-transform gives

( Y(z) (1 + a_1 z^{-1} + a_2 z^{-2}) = X(z) (b_0 + b_1 z^{-1}) )

Thus,

( H(z) = \frac{b_0 + b_1 z^{-1}}{1 + a_1 z^{-1} + a_2 z^{-2}} )

This rational function fully characterizes the system.

Key Observations

1. Convolution in time domain corresponds to multiplication in Z-domain.
2. The system function completely determines system behavior.
3. Poles of ( H(z) ) determine natural response.
4. Zeros of ( H(z) ) shape the frequency response.

Conceptual Summary

This page emphasizes the central role of the system function in discrete-time signal processing. Whether the task is to find output, input, or impulse response, the process reduces to algebraic manipulation in the Z-domain followed by inverse transformation. The Z-transform converts convolution and difference equations into simple algebraic operations, making system analysis systematic and efficient.

Topic: Non-Trivial Poles, Impulse Response, and System Realization

This page discusses non-trivial poles of a system, computation of impulse response from the system function, and the relationship between different algebraic representations of the same system.

Non-Trivial Poles

For a rational system function

( H(z) = \frac{N(z)}{D(z)} )

non-trivial poles are the roots of the denominator polynomial ( D(z) ) excluding any trivial poles at the origin introduced by powers of ( z^{-1} ).

To determine non-trivial poles:

1. Express ( H(z) ) in standard rational form.
2. Factor the denominator.
3. Solve ( D(z) = 0 ).

Impulse Response Determination

The impulse response ( h[n] ) is defined as the output when the input is

( x[n] = \delta[n] )

Since

( X(z) = 1 )

we have

( Y(z) = H(z) )

Thus,

( h[n] = Z^{-1} \{ H(z) \} )

If the denominator contains distinct poles, partial fraction expansion can be applied:

( H(z) = \frac{A_1}{z - p_1} + \frac{A_2}{z - p_2} + \dots )

Each term contributes a time-domain component of the form

( A_i p_i^n u[n] )

for a right-sided ROC.

Repeated Poles

If a pole is repeated, for example

( H(z) = \frac{A}{(z - p)^2} )

then the inverse Z-transform produces terms involving ( n p^n ).

System Output from Impulse Response

Once ( h[n] ) is known, the output for any input ( x[n] ) is

( y[n] = x[n] * h[n] )

Thus, determining the impulse response fully characterizes the system.

Different Algebraic Forms, Same System

The page emphasizes that a system may have different algebraic representations but still correspond to the same impulse response and pole structure.

For example, rewriting

( H(z) )

in terms of positive or negative powers of ( z ) may introduce trivial poles or zeros, but the non-trivial poles determine system dynamics.

Key Observations

1. Non-trivial poles determine the exponential components of ( h[n] ).
2. The impulse response is obtained by inverse Z-transform of ( H(z) ).
3. Distinct poles produce exponential terms.
4. Repeated poles produce polynomial-weighted exponentials.
5. Different algebraic expressions can represent the same system behavior.

Conceptual Understanding

This page reinforces that the impulse response is the fundamental description of an LTI system. The pole locations determine the natural behavior of the system. Once ( h[n] ) is known, all system outputs can be computed via convolution. Non-trivial poles dictate system dynamics, while trivial poles or zeros may arise from representation choices but do not alter fundamental behavior.

Thus, system analysis reduces to identifying poles, determining their multiplicity, and computing the corresponding inverse Z-transform.

Topic: Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) Systems and Inverse Z-Transform Using Contour Integration

This page introduces Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) systems and outlines the inverse Z-transform using contour integration and the residue theorem.

Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) Systems

A system is said to have an infinite impulse response if its impulse response ( h[n] ) extends indefinitely in time.

Consider a general linear constant-coefficient difference equation:

( y[n] = b_0 x[n] + b_1 x[n-1] + \dots + b_M x[n-M] 
- a_1 y[n-1] - a_2 y[n-2] - \dots - a_N y[n-N] )

Because the output depends on previous output samples, the system is recursive.

Taking the Z-transform (assuming zero initial conditions):

( Y(z) (1 + a_1 z^{-1} + \dots + a_N z^{-N}) = X(z) (b_0 + b_1 z^{-1} + \dots + b_M z^{-M}) )

Thus, the system function is

( H(z) = \frac{Y(z)}{X(z)} = \frac{b_0 + b_1 z^{-1} + \dots + b_M z^{-M}}{1 + a_1 z^{-1} + \dots + a_N z^{-N}} )

If the denominator has poles other than at the origin, the impulse response generally continues for all ( n \ge 0 ). Hence, it is an Infinite Impulse Response system.

Inverse Z-Transform Using Contour Integration

The inverse Z-transform can be defined as

( x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi j} \oint_{C} X(z) z^{n-1} dz )

where ( C ) is a closed contour in the ROC.

This expression comes from complex analysis and is evaluated using Cauchy’s integral theorem.

Residue Method

If ( X(z) ) is a rational function with isolated poles inside the contour ( C ), the integral can be evaluated using the residue theorem:

( x[n] = \sum \text{Residues of } X(z) z^{n-1} )

at poles inside the contour.

For a simple pole at ( z = p ), the residue is given by

( \text{Res} = \lim_{z \to p} (z - p) X(z) z^{n-1} )

Thus, each pole contributes a term proportional to ( p^n ).

Analytic Function Condition

Cauchy’s integral theorem states that if a function is analytic (holomorphic) inside and on a closed contour, then

( \oint_{C} f(z) dz = 0 )

The inverse Z-transform integral works because ( X(z) z^{n-1} ) is analytic everywhere except at its poles.

Key Conditions

1. The contour ( C ) must lie within the ROC.
2. The contour must enclose the poles corresponding to the desired sequence.
3. The function must be analytic everywhere inside the contour except at isolated poles.

Conceptual Understanding

This page connects discrete-time signal analysis with complex analysis. The inverse Z-transform is fundamentally a contour integral in the complex plane. In practice, this reduces to the residue method, where each pole contributes an exponential term in time domain.

Thus:

1. IIR systems arise due to recursive difference equations.
2. Poles in the denominator produce infinite impulse responses.
3. The residue theorem provides a systematic way to compute inverse Z-transforms.

This establishes the theoretical foundation for inverse Z-transform computation beyond partial fraction expansion.
